entry.dc:title: COAL MINE DISPOSAL OF FLUE GAS CLEANING WASTES.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.prism:publicationName: Electric Power Research Institute Coal Combustion Systems Division Report EPRI Cs
entry.dc:description: This report summarizes the state-of-the-art of disposal of electric utility flue gas cleaning wastes, defined as fly ash and flue gas desulfurization wastes, in active and abandoned mines, it presents six examples full-scale mine disposal operations, examines the regulations promulgated under the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977, identifies the anticipated effects of the regulations on mine disposal operations, and outlines areas of additional research.

entry.dc:title: AUTOMATIC FIRE PROTECTION SYSTEMS FOR SURFACE MINING EQUIPMENT.
entry.dc:creator: Pomroy W.
entry.prism:publicationName: Information Circular United States Bureau of Mines
entry.dc:description: This report reviews the development and testing of systems for haulage trucks, front end loaders, lcoal augers, dozers, drills, and shovels. A variety of fire sensors, extinguishing agents, and control systems are discussed.

entry.dc:title: STRUCTURE RESPONSE AND DAMAGE PRODUCED BY AIRBLAST FROM SURFACE MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Siskind D.
entry.prism:publicationName: Report of Investigations United States Bureau of Mines
entry.dc:description: The Bureau of Mines studied airblast to assess its damage and annoyance potential, and to determine safe levels and appropriate measurement techniques. Safe levels of airblast were 134 dBL (0. 1 Hz), 133 dBL (2 Hz), 129 dBL (6 Hz), and 105 dB C-slow.

entry.dc:title: EFFECTS OF COAL MINE SUBSIDENCE IN THE SHERIDAN, WYOMING, AREA.
entry.dc:creator: Dunrud C.
entry.prism:publicationName: United States Department of the Interior Geological Survey Professional Papers
entry.dc:description: Analyses of the surface effects of past underground coal mining in the Sheridan, Wyoming, area suggest that underground mining of strippable coal deposits may damage the environment more over long periods of time than would modern surface mining, provided proper restoration procedures are followed after surface mining. Subsidence depressions and pits are a continuing hazard to the environment and to man's activities in the Sheridan, Wyo. , area. This report discusses the geology, subsidence and other effects of past and present mining in this area, as related to the environment, coal resource management, and land use.

entry.dc:title: Environmental effects of surface mining of minerals other than coal: annotated bibliography and summary report.
entry.dc:creator: Richardson B.
entry.prism:publicationName: General Technical Report Forest Service US Dept Agriculture

Contains results of an extensive computer-based literature search and responses to a national survey. Each reference is indexed by commodity, general subject, and environmental problem. The publication includes a section of references to unpublished literature and a summary of professional concerns about mining impacts throughout the U.S.-from Authors

entry.dc:title: Regulatory Alert: Regulation of Coal mining
entry.dc:creator: Deland M.
entry.dc:description: The Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 (SMCRA) thus far has received much less public attention than other federal environmental statutes such as the Clean Air and Water Acts of 1977 and the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act of 1976 enacted during the same period. Yet SMCRA, which is administered by the Department of Interior rather than by EPA, is equally complex and controversial and directly governs how our increasingly valuable coal resources can be mined. The act established the Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement (OSM) and granted it authority to regulate both surface coal mining and the surface effects of underground coal mining. © 1980, American Chemical Society. entry.dc:title: Effects of topsoil storage during surface mining on the viability of VA mycorrhiza
entry.dc:creator: Rives C.S.
entry.dc:description: Storing topsoil for 3 years was shown to reduce substantially the levels of viable inocula relative to levels in adjacent, undisturbed prairie soils. The detrimental effect of storage on VA mycorrhiza is associated with the loss of viability of mycorrhizal fragments occurring in the stored soil. Data are also presented supporting an interaction between infected root segments and roots of uninfected plants as a major means of spreading mycorrhiza in these soils. © 1980 The Williams & Wilkins Co.

entry.dc:title: IMPACT OF MINING ACTIVITIES ON WATER QUALITY IN WESTERN NORTH CAROLINA
entry.dc:creator: Duda A.
entry.prism:publicationName: Jawra Journal of the American Water Resources Association
entry.dc:description: ABSTRACT: An intensive water quality investigation was conducted in western North Carolina to determine whether water quality problems existed from point and nonpoint source inputs of sediment from surface mining activities. Depth integrated measurements of sediment transport and biological sampling of benthic communities indicated that very serious water quality problems were caused by erosion from a concentrated area of open pit mining for mica, kaolin, and feldspar. The erosion occurred on haul roads, active mines, inactive mines, and tailings disposal piles. The need for using specific “Best Management Practices” for erosion control on the mining operation is discussed. These practices need to be implemented to restore populations of trout to the degraded reaches of the river. Additional monitoring data are presented that indicate that the biological integrity of surface waters can be preserved in the vicinity of point source mining discharges when the operators utilize proper practices in settling and neutralizing their effluent. While much has been done to abate the point source discharges, attention now needs to be focused on the nonpoint sources of sediment from mining operations. Copyright © 1980, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

entry.dc:title: Implementation of US Surface Mine and Reclamation Act
entry.dc:creator: Sani E.
entry.dc:description: The US Congress is currently studying various ways through which legislation similar to that of the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977— which is concerned mainly with coal, can be applied to all minerals other than coal. This study analyses three US mineral industries—copper, iron ore, and phosphate rock - and identifies a number of areas which Congress and other decision makers ought to consider in arriving at such legislation. The author concludes that reclamation costs may affect the economic and financial performance of each of these industries in a different manner; furthermore, their economic behaviour is significantly different from that of coal. The author's main recommendation is that if surface mining regulations are to be legislated, they should be industry- and commodity-specific rather than umbrella legislation for all non-coal minerals. © 1980, All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: ( Recultivation of areas devastated by mining of calcium phosphate).
entry.dc:creator: Karlowitsch S.
entry.dc:description: On an area where surface mining of calcium phosphate had been carried out, red clover, white clover, timothy, cocksfoot, maize, oats and potatoes were grown on 1) the topsoil or 2) the underlying glacuonite sand, which contained more P, K and trace elements and had a higher pH. Without fertilizer, red clover and white clover yielded more on 2) than on 1). Potato yields were similar on both substrates. Grass and cereal yields were low and less on 2) than on 1). Yield responses of grasses and cereals to NPK were greater on 2) than on 1). Oat yields were increased 5.9 and 2.1 times and maize yields 10.9 and 2.3 times on 2) and 1), respectively. The clovers showed smaller responses to NPK. N had most influence on yield, especially on 2) where P and K had scarcely any effect.-from Field Crop Abstracts

entry.dc:title: An inventory of particulate emissions from open sources
entry.dc:creator: Evans J.S.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of the Air Pollution Control Association
entry.dc:description: Open sources are those stationary sources of air pollution too great in extent to be controlled through enclosure or ducting. Open sources of atmospheric particles include: wind erosion, tilling, and prescribed burning of agricultural cropland; surface mining and wind erosion of tailings piles; vehicular travel on both paved and unpaved roads; construction site activity; and forest fires. It is estimated that in 1976 the total open source emissions of particles in the U.S. amounted to over 580 × 10<sup>6</sup> ton. These estimates indicate that emissions from the two largest open source classes, travel on unpaved roads and agricultural wind erosion, accounted for 86% of this total. The open source emissions in ten states (AZ, CA, KS, MN, MT, NM, ND, OH, SD, TX) contributed 6 2% of the national emissions for 1976. © 1980 Air & Waste Management Association.

entry.dc:title: Coal problems and prospects.
entry.dc:creator: Van Rensburg W.C.J.
entry.prism:publicationName: University of Texas Bureau of Economic Geology Mineral Resources Circular
entry.dc:description: Outlines the National Energy Plan as it pertains to coal as a potential major energy source and describes how production constraints may make the NEP's 1985 goal of l,265 million tons of coal unobtainable. The authors review constraints such as regulations on mining, health and safety and air quality control solid waste disposal problems, and needs regarding labor, transportation, and capital. They also point up the need for new conversion processes and for continued research and development in pollution control, gasification, liquefaction, and deep surface mining. Also reviews the impact of President Carter's latest energy program and the benefits to coal production from his proposed excess profits tax on the oil industry. Tabular material covers the additional mines, equipment, and transportation needed to reach the NEP goal, estimated coal consumption in Texas and the nation, capital required for such consumption, and capital and operating costs of environmental controls on new coal-fired power plants. Make's specific recommendations for realizing the potential of coal as a major energy source, recommending the formulation of a consistent environmental policy, immediate construction of gasification and liquefaction plants, and a thorough review of all regulations that impede the development of coal mines and utilization plants. -Authors

entry.dc:title: FUEL COSTS ARE CAUSING CHANGES IN SURFACE MINING METHODS.

entry.dc:description: The article illustrates several instances where rising fuel costs are causing changes. Machinery can in many instances be switched from diesel to electric-powered. As fuel costs escalate at a rate far exceeding that of electricity costs, the balance will swing to increased utilization of electricity.

entry.dc:title: Aerial survey techniques for locating abandoned strip mine land
entry.dc:creator: Dattavio L.
entry.dc:description: The Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act required that states develop regulatory programs and reclamation plans for surface mining activities. Prior to passage of this law, the Indiana legislature required Indiana Department of Natural Resources (IDNR) to survey abandoned mine lands not under the control of state reclamation laws. IDNR then contracted the Laboratory for Applications of Remote Sensing (LARS) at Purdue University to conduct a preliminary survey of these lands. Photointerpretation techniques of medium scale color infrared photography enabled the LARS staff to identify partially reclaimed and nonreclaimed sites within a 20-county area in southwestern Indiana. Over 4,700 ha of abandoned lands were located and classified on the aerial photography. This information is currently being used by IDNR to develop reclamation plants to revegetate the abandoned lands. The results of this survey clearly indicate that photointerpretation is an effective technique to complete initial inventories of nonreclaimed mine lands.
